html:
The Gur-e-Amir, "tomb of the king", is the mausoleum of Timur in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. It was begun in 1403.

Timur first had it built for his beloved grandson and heir, Muhammad Sultan, who died in 1403. Timur himself died in 1405 on campaign toward China and was buried here. His son Shah Rukh, his grandson Ulugh Beg and his teacher also lie inside.

The building is crowned by a tall ribbed dome, shaped a little like a melon, covered in turquoise and blue tiles and raised on a high drum. Ulugh Beg placed over Timur's grave a slab of dark green jade, then said to be the largest piece of jade in the world.

In June 1941 a Soviet team opened Timur's tomb to study his skeleton. Two days later Germany invaded the Soviet Union, giving rise to a legend of a curse.

The Gur-e-Amir became a model for the great tombs of the Mughal Empire, whose rulers descended from Timur through Babur. Its plan and dome look forward to Humayun's Tomb in Delhi and to the Taj Mahal, the subject of Taj Mahal begun.
sum: The Gur-e-Amir, "tomb of the king", is the mausoleum of Timur in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. It was begun in 1403.
